## What is a "factor"? {.smaller}

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="55%"}
A **factor** is a long–short stock portfolio:

::: {.incremental}
- **Size**: small firms − big firms
- **Value**: cheap − expensive stocks
- **Profitability**: robust − weak profits
- **Investment**: conservative − aggressive investors
- **Momentum**: past winners − past losers
- **Market**: all stocks − T-bills
:::
:::
::: {.column width="45%"}
Their long-run average return is the **risk premium** used in asset pricing and investing.

<br>

**But:** a 60-year average may hide very different behaviour in good and bad times.
:::
::::

::: {.notes}
About 45 seconds. These six factors are the standard building blocks of empirical asset pricing (Fama–French five factors plus momentum). Each is a zero-cost portfolio, so its return is a pure "premium".
:::

## Questions

1. Are factor premia different in **recessions** vs. expansions?
2. Do premia change after months of **high market stress** (VIX)?
3. Have premia **shrunk since they were published**?

::: {.notes}
About 30 seconds. Q1 is descriptive, Q2 uses information known in advance (lagged VIX), Q3 connects to the debate on whether publishing an anomaly makes it disappear (McLean & Pontiff 2016).
:::

## Wrangling challenge: French's CSV files {.smaller}

The files mix text, a monthly block and an annual block, so `read_csv()` alone fails.

```{.r code-line-numbers="2|4-7|11-14"}
parse_french_csv <- function(path) {
  lines <- read_lines(path)
  # header row is the first line starting with a comma
  header_idx <- which(str_detect(lines, "^\\s*,"))[1]
  body       <- lines[(header_idx + 1):length(lines)]
  is_month   <- str_detect(body, "^\\s*\\d{6}\\s*,")
  body       <- body[seq_len(which(!is_month)[1] - 1)]
  col_names  <- str_trim(str_split_1(lines[header_idx], ","))
  col_names[1] <- "yyyymm"

  read_csv(I(paste(body, collapse = "\n")), col_names = col_names,
           na = c("-99.99", "-999")) |>
    mutate(date = ymd(paste0(yyyymm, "01")), .before = 1) |>
    select(-yyyymm)
}
```

::: {.notes}
About 1 minute. This is the "challenge / lesson" slide. Step through the highlighted lines: read raw lines, find the header, keep only the monthly rows, then parse. Lesson: writing one small, tested function was faster and more reliable than hand-editing the CSVs, and it means the project updates automatically when French posts new data.
:::

## Recessions vs. expansions {.smaller}

```{r}
panel |>
  mutate(regime = if_else(usrec == 1, "Recession", "Expansion")) |>
  summarise_premia(regime) |>
  select(factor, regime, mean_ann, t_stat) |>
  pivot_wider(names_from = regime, values_from = c(mean_ann, t_stat),
              names_glue = "{regime}_{.value}") |>
  select(factor, starts_with("Expansion"), starts_with("Recession")) |>
  gt(rowname_col = "factor") |>
  tab_spanner("Expansion", columns = starts_with("Expansion")) |>
  tab_spanner("Recession", columns = starts_with("Recession")) |>
  cols_label(Expansion_mean_ann = "Mean %/yr", Expansion_t_stat = "t",
             Recession_mean_ann = "Mean %/yr", Recession_t_stat = "t") |>
  fmt_number(columns = matches("mean_ann|t_stat"), decimals = 2) |>
  tab_options(table.font.size = "80%")
```

::: {.notes}
About 1 minute. Read off the two or three biggest differences. Remind the audience that recessions are only about 1 month in 7, so recession estimates are noisy.
:::

## After high-stress months (VIX)

```{r}
#| fig-width: 9
#| fig-height: 5
vix_panel <- panel |> filter(!is.na(vix_lag))
vix_cuts  <- quantile(unique(vix_panel[c("date", "vix_lag")])$vix_lag,
                      c(0, 1/3, 2/3, 1))
vix_panel |>
  mutate(vix_regime = cut(vix_lag, breaks = vix_cuts, include.lowest = TRUE,
                          labels = c("Low", "Medium", "High"))) |>
  group_by(factor, vix_regime) |>
  summarise(mean = 12 * mean(ret), se = 12 * sd(ret) / sqrt(n()),
            .groups = "drop") |>
  mutate(lo = mean - 1.96 * se, hi = mean + 1.96 * se) |>
  plot_vix_regimes()
```

::: {.notes}
About 1 minute. Uses last month's VIX, so this is information an investor actually had. Point to which factors' intervals move away from zero in high-VIX months.
:::

## Many models: one regression per factor {.smaller}

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="40%"}
```{.r}
panel |>
  group_by(factor) |>
  nest() |>
  mutate(
    model = map(data, \(d)
      lm(ret ~ usrec +
           term_spread_lag,
         data = d)),
    coefs = map(model, tidy,
                conf.int = TRUE))
```
:::
::: {.column width="60%"}
```{r}
#| fig-width: 7
#| fig-height: 4.5
panel |>
  filter(!is.na(term_spread_lag)) |>
  fit_by_factor(ret ~ usrec + term_spread_lag) |>
  select(factor, coefs) |>
  unnest(coefs) |>
  filter(term != "(Intercept)") |>
  plot_coefs()
```
:::
::::

::: {.notes}
About 1 minute. Same model, six factors, no copy-paste. Left panel: recession effect holding the yield curve fixed. Right panel: does last month's term spread predict this month's return?
:::

## Takeaways

::: {.incremental}
- **Recessions:** market premium flips from +9% to −7% per year, momentum vanishes; investment does *better* (+8.7%)
- **High VIX:** market earns most afterwards, momentum earns nothing (crash risk)
- **Publication:** all 5 anomaly premia shrink afterwards; size and investment nearly disappear
- **Lesson:** reusable functions + one processed dataset kept the report and slides consistent and fully reproducible
:::

<br>

Report, code and data: **OCN 682 GitHub organization → ocn682-factor-regimes**

::: {.notes}
About 45 seconds, then questions. Main message: a single 60-year average hides big differences across economic conditions and over time.
:::
